list.listitem: The well-adult exam is a visit with a clinician that focuses on health promotion, screening, and prevention. Some insurance companies reimburse for an annual health office visit; however, not all screenings should be done on an annual basis. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) provides evidence-based recommendations for screenings and counseling on many topics.

An updated Cochrane review found that general health checks have little or no effect on total mortality. In this update, the authors defined health checks as "screening for more than one disease or risk factor in more than one organ system". The studies included in the meta-analysis were more recent, limited to 2012 and onwards. The authors concluded that the benefits of general health checks are not likely, however clinicians should continue clinically driven testing and preventive activities .

A recent study compared cancer screening recommendations across countries with well developed economies. Common themes included colorectal cancer screening using primarily the fecal immunochemical test, cervical cancer screening beginning at age 21 to 25, biennial mammography between the ages of 50 and 69, and few recommendations favoring routine prostate cancer screening. The intensity of screening was not clearly associated with GDP. See the article for links to the sources of screening recommendations for the 25 studied industrialized countries.
Recommendations for the United States, UK, Canada, Germany and Italy are summarized below with links to the most recent version of these recommendations.

In an effort to grade the strength of the recommendation, the USPSTF provides a letter grade of A, B, C, D, or I, defined as follows where "net benefit" is benefit minus harm:
Grade A: High certainty that the net benefit is substantial Grade B: High certainty that the new benefit is moderate or moderate certainty that the net benefit is moderate to substantial Grade C: At least moderate certainty that the net benefit is small Grade D: Moderate or high certainty that the service has no net benefit or that the harms outweight the benefits Grade I: Current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of the service

The USPSTF recommends that the clinician discuss level A and B recommendations and offer them as priority during the well-adult exam. These recommendations are regularly updated. For the most recent recommendations by topic, see this USPSTF site.

When providing guidance to an individual patient, use the electronic preventive services selector (ePSS), which personalizes recommendations based on age, sex, tobacco use, pregnancy, and whether the person is sexually active.
App versions of the ePSS are also available for Android and iPhone.

Even though the suggested screening options are acceptable, they should not be regarded as equivalent. The clinician should discuss the potential advantages and disadvantages of each screening option with patients before choosing a screening method. For example, the benefit in terms of years of life saved and cancer deaths prevented is similar for the different recommended approaches to colorectal cancer screening, their costs and potential harms vary considerably.
Clinicians should discourage screenings with level D recommendations, unless there are mitigating considerations.

The clinician should not routinely offer services given a priority of level C unless there is an individualized reason to do so. In some cases, such as for breast cancer screening for women in their 40s, the balance of benefits and harms may depend on both a patient's individual risk and how they value potential benefits and harms.

For services with level I recommendations, the clinician should discuss with patients the uncertainty of benefit surrounding these services or the population they serve. For example, the recommendation regarding screening for autism is an "I" because there have been no clinical trials comparing screening to no screening, and because all treatment trials had enrolled patients with moderate to severe autism. If a physician believes that parents may not reliably identify or report behavioral symptoms consistent with autism, then screening may be appropriate.
